planting.note: Plant certified seed tubers once soil has warmed past hard-frost danger; Zīle is a mid-late Baltic-bred variety that does not need a long warm season to finish.

directions: Zīle is a mid-late maturing table potato bred at Latvia's State Priekuļi Plant Breeding Institute and officially released in 1984, part of a continuous potato-breeding program at Priekuļi dating to 1931. Latvian agronomy literature describes its tubers as oval with light yellow skin and flesh and moderately high starch content, and growers have noted it for solid disease resistance and good storage life, which keeps it in home-garden use in Latvia today. Plant whole or cut seed tubers in hilled rows after the soil has warmed, keeping moisture even through tuber set, since this Baltic-bred variety is adapted to a relatively short, cool growing season.
sources: Latvia University of Life Sciences and Technologies — Agronomijas Vēstis (Latvian Journal of Agronomy), potato variety evaluation trials
ScienceDirect — Nutritional composition of freshly harvested and stored Latvian potato varieties
State Priekuļi Plant Breeding Institute variety records

planting.note: Plant individual cloves in autumn so they root before ground freeze; bred for Lithuania's cold continental climate.

directions: Dangiai is a hardneck garlic cultivar bred from Lithuania's local garlic genetic resources at the Institute of Horticulture of the Lithuanian Research Centre for Agriculture and Forestry, selected for reliable winter survival in the country's cold continental climate. Bulbs typically form five to seven large cloves beneath white outer scales streaked with purple, and the cultivar is noted in Lithuanian trial records for good productivity and storage life. Plant cloves root-down in autumn, mulch over winter, and let the foliage die back naturally the following summer before lifting and curing bulbs for long-term storage.
sources: Plants (MDPI journal) — Application of Genetic Resources in the Development of New Lithuanian Vegetable Cultivars
Lithuanian Research Centre for Agriculture and Forestry, Institute of Horticulture

planting.note: Long-day onion bred for northern latitudes; start indoors well before the last frost for northern gardens.

directions: Joriai is a medium-early storage onion bred from Lithuanian genetic resources at the Institute of Horticulture of the Lithuanian Research Centre for Agriculture and Forestry, reaching maturity roughly 90 to 110 days after germination. Trial descriptions note medium-sized bulbs with yellowish-brown outer skin and white flesh, vigorous green foliage of seven to eight leaves, and good cold tolerance paired with notably strong keeping quality in storage. Start seed indoors in late winter, transplant out once the soil is workable, and cure bulbs thoroughly after tops fall over to make the most of their long storage life.
sources: Plants (MDPI journal) — Application of Genetic Resources in the Development of New Lithuanian Vegetable Cultivars

planting.note: Plant tuber pieces in a permanent bed around last frost; any fragment left behind will resprout the following year.

directions: Sauliai is a Lithuanian-bred Jerusalem artichoke cultivar that, in a comparative Lithuanian field trial of several cultivars, produced the heaviest average individual tubers of the group (roughly 26 grams each) and the highest crude protein content, with white-skinned tubers and the species' usual tall, coarse, sunflower-like growth topped by small yellow flowers in late summer. Plant tuber pieces in a dedicated, contained bed in full sun, since the species spreads readily from any tuber left in the ground. Dig after frost kills the foliage, continuing to harvest into winter, since cold exposure sweetens the tubers' nutty flavor.
sources: Žemės ūkio mokslai (Lithuanian Journal of Agricultural Sciences) — comparative quality study of Jerusalem artichoke cultivars
Plants (MDPI journal) — Application of Genetic Resources in the Development of New Lithuanian Vegetable Cultivars

common_name: Chemlal Olive (Chemlal de Kabylie, Algeria's Dominant Oil Olive)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Chemlal sets a better crop with a compatible second cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Chemlal, also called Chemlal de Kabylie, is Algeria's single most widely planted olive cultivar, concentrated in the Kabylie highlands and grown almost exclusively for oil. Molecular studies of the official Algerian olive germplasm collection confirm it as a cultivar genetically distinct from Tunisia's similarly named Chemlali, despite the two frequently being confused with each other. Plant grafted trees in full sun and well-drained soil, interplanting with a compatible cultivar for reliable cross-pollination, and expect a long juvenile period typical of olives. Harvest as fruit darkens in late autumn for pressing; Chemlal tolerates the cooler, wetter winters of Kabylie's foothill orchards better than some of Algeria's drought-adapted western cultivars.
sources: International Olive Council — World Catalogue of Olive Varieties
Molecular Analysis of the Official Algerian Olive Collection Highlighted a Hotspot of Biodiversity in the Central Mediterranean Basin (PMC)
Physico-chemical and sensory evaluation of virgin olive oils from several Algerian olive-growing regions

common_name: Boussera (Limonette de Marrakech, Moroccan Preserved-Lemon Citron)

planting.note: Plant container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this limetta-type citrus is cold-sensitive and needs frost protection in marginal zones.

directions: Boussera, catalogued formally by the University of California Riverside's Citrus Variety Collection as Marrakech Limonette, is one of Morocco's two indigenous lemon-type citrus fruits traditionally used, alongside the thinner-skinned Doqq, to make the country's salt-cured preserved lemons for tagines. The medium-sized, ribbed fruit carries a thin, light yellowish-orange rind and very sour, aromatic pale-yellow flesh, borne on a vigorous, lightly spiny tree with purple-tinged new growth that flowers and fruits nearly year-round. It has seen little commercial orchard cultivation even within Morocco and survives mainly in dooryard plantings and citrus germplasm collections. Grow it like other acid citrus in full sun with well-drained soil, sheltering it from frost, and expect the sourest, most aromatic fruit among Morocco's traditional preserved-lemon varieties.
sources: University of California Riverside — Citrus Variety Collection (CRC 3989, Marrakech Limonette)
Taste of Maroc — Moroccan culinary reference on Doqq and Boussera lemon varieties

common_name: Jerid Pepper (Tunisian Oasis-Region Hot Pepper Landrace)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost and transplant out only once nights have warmed, since this landrace comes from Tunisia's hot southern oases.

directions: Jerid is a hot pepper landrace named for Tunisia's Jerid (Djerid) oasis region in the country's south, one of four Tunisian landraces compared in a published horticultural performance and quality trial. In that study it had by far the highest capsaicinoid (pungency) content and the highest vitamin E (tocopherol) content of the four landraces tested, though its yield ran more moderate than some of the milder comparison lines. Grow it like other Capsicum annuum peppers, starting seed indoors well ahead of the last frost and setting plants out only once nights stay reliably warm, and give it full sun. Having been grown for generations at the hot, dry edge of Tunisia's southern oases, it should handle heat and brief drought stress better than pepper cultivars selected for cooler, wetter climates.
sources: Horticultural performance and functional quality traits of four hot pepper landraces from Tunisia (TURSTEP journal)
INRAT (Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique de Tunisie) germplasm trials
